active.text: How does a mechanical watch run all day and night with zero battery? Every time you move your wrist, a hidden weight coils a flat steel spring inside, and a tiny rhythmic brake meters up to forty-two hours of stored power out to the hands.
Start with everyday wrist motion. Every move of your arm swings the heavy orange half-moon rotor around its center pin. About eight hundred forty swings wind the watch from empty all the way to full.

As the rotor turns, it winds a flat blued spring tight inside the brass mainspring barrel. Fully coiled to seven tight turns, that single spring stores up to forty-two hours of power — six hours for every turn.

So what stops that coiled spring from dumping all its power in two seconds? The oscillating balance wheel and tiny rocking pallet lever act like a steady brake, catching the escape wheel and releasing just one tooth at a time — eight gentle ticks every second.

Those fast ticks feed inward through a train of meshed brass gears. Each small steel pinion turns a much larger brass wheel on the next shaft, stepping the speed down cleanly for seconds, minutes, and hours.

Three concentric shafts carry those three steady speeds right up through the open exhibition dial to sweep the watch hands. Eight tiny steps each second give a mechanical watch its smooth gliding sweep.

Finally, take the watch off and leave it sitting still on a nightstand. It drains one hour of reserve for every hour it sits — after forty-two hours, the coiled spring unwinds completely and the balance wheel rests still. No battery is dead; just pick it up and wear it again.
